answer: The authors recorded activity from mature granule neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG) using two-photon calcium imaging while mice walked on a moving treadmill equipped with spatial cues. To quantify spatial information, they mapped calcium activity traces to the animal's position to generate a tuning vector. The mean calcium signal at each location was computed for every neuron and normalized to the time spent at that position. The modulus of this tuning vector served as a spatial tuning index reflecting place-specificity. Additionally, the authors utilized decoding accuracy to reflect spatial information content, noting that neuronal activity from large populations can be used to decode an animal's position within an environment. They assessed the effects of manipulating adult neurogenesis on this DG spatial information content.

Instead, the authors found that silencing ABNs reduces population sparsity throughout hippocampal subfields. These findings appear to be in disagreement with ours, although this could be due to methodological differences: electrophysiology vs. Ca2+ imaging recordings in our work, different genetic drivers targeting newborn ABNs (Nestin-Cre vs. Ascl1-Cre-ERT2), different measures of information content (mutual information vs. Fisher information) and our use of EE.

[Ablating adult neurogenesis reduces single cell activity and tuning] To assess how single cell spatial information changes in the DG, we mapped the calcium activity traces to the position of the mouse on the treadmill to generate a tuning vector (Fig. 3a, b). The mean calcium signal at each location was computed for every neuron and normalized to the time the mouse spent at that position. The modulus of the tuning vector was used as a spatial tuning index that reflects the place-specificity of activity29.

[Discussion] These findings appear to be in disagreement with ours, although this could be due to methodological differences: electrophysiology vs. Ca2+ imaging recordings in our work, different genetic drivers targeting newborn ABNs (Nestin-Cre vs. Ascl1-Cre-ERT2), different measures of information content (mutual information vs. Fisher information) and our use of EE. Although electrophysiological recordings directly record action potentials with much higher temporal resolution than in vivo Ca2+ imaging, the sparse nature of DG activity makes these recordings particularly challenging, resulting in relatively fewer single-unit recordings in DG, which may be reflected in the fact that the strongest effects of silencing ABNs were found in CA3 and CA1. In another study using in vivo Ca2+ imaging, Tuncdemir et al. found that ablating or silencing ABNs does not alter population-level fraction of active cells (i.e. sparsity), mean firing rates or spatial information/tuning properties during the formation of cognitive maps64, which differs from our work and partially differs from the data of McHugh et al. Again, differences in the experimental and analysis methods could account for the different findings: a different implantation surgery that requires the partial removal of CA1, a rewarded treadmill task, and different methods to estimate Ca2+ activity and spatial information.

[Introduction] But even neurons that are not selectively tuned to a single place can contribute to the spatial information encoded in neural populations. Neuronal activity recordings from large populations can be used to decode the position of an animal within an environment23,24, with the decoding accuracy reflecting the spatial information content. These neural representations of space are essential for spatial memory, as was recently demonstrated25.

[Introduction] We recorded activity from mature granule neurons in the DG using two-photon calcium imaging, as the mice walked on a moving treadmill with spatial cues. To directly demonstrate the role of adult neurogenesis in the DG neural code, we either chronically ablated DG neurogenesis by focal irradiation of the hippocampus, or acutely silenced immature ABNs using chemogenetics, and assessed the effect of these manipulations on DG spatial information content. We found that EE-exposure results in increased spatial information content in the DG, and that this increase requires immature ABNs.

[Introduction] Yet, it is unclear how this would affect neural representations of space during the formation of a new memory, as the animal explores a novel environment. To address these open questions, we investigated whether increasing adult neurogenesis by housing mice in an enriched environment (EE) would change the DG spatial code. We recorded activity from mature granule neurons in the DG using two-photon calcium imaging, as the mice walked on a moving treadmill with spatial cues.
